summary: This RFC specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, a successor to the original 1822 protocol between hosts and the ARPANET packet switches. It lets hosts address each other with logical identifiers as well as the physical interface identifiers used by 1822.

plainLanguage.summary:
On the ARPANET, a host was named by the port it was plugged into. RFC 878 adds a second kind of name that says nothing about where the host is, so a host can move and several hosts can share one port.

A host tells its IMP which names it wants to use, and the IMP works out the physical address to send to when a message arrives for that name.

what is the arpanet 1822l host access protocol
subtitle: How ARPANET hosts were given logical names instead of physical port numbers.

tldr.problem: On the ARPANET, a host could only be addressed by the physical port it was plugged into, so moving a host or letting several hosts share a port was awkward.
tldr.mechanism: The 1822L protocol gives a host a 16-bit logical name. The host declares the names it wants to use to its IMP in a Name Declaration Message, and the IMP translates a name into a physical address using one of three policies when it sends a message or opens a virtual circuit.
tldr.outcome: Hosts using the old 1822 protocol and hosts using 1822L can talk to each other, because the IMPs translate the leader and address formats automatically. RFC 878 obsoleted RFC 851.

facts.label: Hosts addressable by an 1822L address
facts.value: Host numbers 0 to 63 at IMPs 1 to 255

today: RFC 878 is an ARPANET document from December 1983 and has not been obsoleted. It updated and obsoleted RFC 851, and the changes it made to that document are marked with revision bars in the right margin.

sections.title: Why 1822L Existed
sections.content:
RFC 878 specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, which lets hosts use logical addressing, meaning host names that are independent of their physical location on the ARPANET, to communicate with each other. The protocol is a successor to the existing 1822 Host Access Protocol, which is described in sections 3.3 and 3.4 of BBN Report 1822. Although 1822L uses different host-to-IMP leaders than 1822, the IMPs continue to support 1822, and hosts using either protocol can communicate with each other because the IMPs handle the translation automatically.

The main differences between the two protocols are the format of the leaders used to introduce messages between a host and an IMP, and the way the source and destination hosts are specified in those leaders. A host chooses between the two protocols: when it comes up on an IMP it declares itself an 1822 or an 1822L host by the type of NOP message it uses, and once up it can switch by issuing another NOP. Hosts that do not use 1822L remain addressable by, and able to communicate with, hosts that do, and the other way round.

One further difference is that the 1822 leaders are symmetric while the 1822L leaders are not. In 1822 the same leader format is used for messages in both directions between a host and its IMP, so a leader sent over a cable looped back onto itself would arrive looking like a legal message from a real host. The 1822L headers are not symmetric, so a host can detect that its connection to its IMP is looped by receiving a message with the wrong leader format, and take appropriate action.
sections.plainLanguage: The ARPANET host access protocol is the interface between a host and the packet-switching node it is plugged into. 1822L changes that interface so that a host can be called by a name that does not say where it is.

sections.title: Names, Addresses and Their Formats
sections.content:
The 1822 protocol defines one form of host specification and 1822L defines two more: 1822 addresses, 1822L names and 1822L addresses.

An 1822 address is the 24-bit host address found in 1822 leaders. It is made of an 8-bit host number and a 16-bit IMP number. These fields are large, and the ARPANET never used more than a fraction of the available address space. 1822 addresses are used in 1822 leaders only.

An 1822L name is a 16-bit unsigned number that serves as a logical identifier for one or more hosts. The names are 16-bit unsigned numbers except that bits 1 and 2 are not both zero, which allows over 49,000 hosts to be specified.

1822 addresses cannot be used in 1822L leaders, but an 1822L host may still need to address a specific physical host port or an IMP fake host, and 1822L addresses exist for that. An 1822L address is a subset of the 1822L name space with both bits 1 and 2 off: bits 1 and 2 are zero, bits 3 to 8 carry the host number and bits 9 to 16 the IMP number. This format lets 1822L hosts address hosts 0 to 63 at IMPs 1 to 255, because IMP 0 does not exist. The highest host numbers are reserved for the IMP's internal fake hosts; at the time of writing the IMP had seven fake hosts, so host numbers 57 to 63 addressed the fake hosts and 0 to 56 addressed real hosts external to the IMP.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to name a host: the old 24-bit address that says exactly which port it is on, a 16-bit logical name, and a 16-bit address that also says which port it is on but fits inside the new format.

sections.title: How Names Become Authorized and Effective
sections.content:
Every host on a C/30 IMP, whether it uses 1822 or 1822L to reach the network, can have one or more 1822L names. Because of implementation constraints, hosts on non-C/30 IMPs cannot be assigned 1822L names, and 1822L hosts use 1822L addresses to reach all other hosts instead.

Names are assigned by a central network administrator. When a name is created it is assigned to a host, or a group of hosts, at one or more specific host ports, and the host is allowed to reside at those ports and nowhere else. If a host moves it keeps the same name, but the administrator has to update the central database, and the changes are distributed to the IMPs by the Network Operations Center. Once the correspondence between a name and the host ports where it may be used has been made official, the name is said to be authorized. 1822L addresses, which refer to physical host ports, are always authorized in this sense.

An IMP cannot tell which host has just come up on a port, because several hosts may share the port and one host may prefer different names at different times. The host therefore has to declare itself before it can send and receive messages, by sending a Name Declaration Message listing the names it would like to be known by. The IMP checks its tables to see whether each name is authorized, and replies with an NDM Reply saying which names are actually authorized and can now be used, which the RFC calls effective. A host can send another NDM at any time to change its list of effective names, adding to it or deleting from it, with the single constraint that a name can only become effective if it is authorized.

A host that comes up using the 1822 protocol is handled differently: the IMP automatically makes the first name it finds in its tables for that host effective when it receives the first 1822 NOP from the host, so even an 1822 host can receive messages from 1822L hosts via its 1822L name. Whenever a host goes down its names automatically become non-effective, and they have to be made effective again when it comes back up.
sections.plainLanguage: An administrator decides which logical names may be used at which ports, and the IMPs are told. When a host starts up it tells the IMP which of those names it wants to use right now, and the IMP answers with the ones that are allowed to become active.

sections.title: Translation Policies
sections.content:
Several hosts can share the same 1822L name. If more than one of them is up at the same time, any message sent to that name is delivered to just one of the hosts sharing it, and an RFNM is returned as usual, but the sending host gets no indication of which host received it and later messages to that name are not guaranteed to go to the same host. Hosts that provide exactly the same service can share a name in this way.

When a host is multi-homed, meaning it uses more than one port to reach the network, the same 1822L name may refer to more than one host port. If the host is up on only one of those ports, that port is used for all messages addressed to it. If it were up on more than one port, the message would be delivered over just one of them, chosen by the subnet, and the choice could change from message to message. A host that wants certain messages delivered on a specific port can use that port's 1822L address or a specific 1822L name that refers to that port alone.

Three address selection policies are available for the name mapping, and each name is assigned one of them in advance. The first tries each translation in the order the physical addresses are listed in the IMP's translation tables and takes the first reachable one, with the list always searched from the top; this is the most commonly used policy. The second selects the closest physical address, using the IMP's routing tables to find the translation to the destination IMP with the least delay path. The third uses load levelling: it is like the second, but the search for a valid translation starts at the address after the one where the previous search ended, which spreads the load from any one IMP's hosts across the host ports associated with a name. The RFC notes that this is not network-wide load levelling, which would need a distributed algorithm and tables.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message goes to a logical name, the IMP has to pick one physical host to send it to. The RFC offers three ways to pick: try the list in order, pick the closest one, or pick the next one in the list each time so the work is spread out.

sections.title: Bringing Up a Host and Counting Replies
sections.content:
When a host comes up on an IMP, or after a break in the communications between them, the orderly flow of messages has to be re-established. The first messages a host should send are three NOP messages. Three are required so that at least one is properly read by the IMP: the first NOP could be concatenated to a previous message if communications had been broken mid-stream, and the third gives redundancy for the second. These NOPs synchronize the IMP with the host, tell the IMP how much padding the host needs between the leader and the body, and tell the IMP whether the host will use 1822 or 1822L leaders. The IMP answers with six NOPs, alternating three 1822 NOPs with three 1822L NOPs, followed by two Interface Reset messages, one of each style. A host that comes up using the 1822 protocol is handled differently: the IMP automatically makes the first name it finds in its tables for that host effective when it receives the first 1822 NOP from the host.

When a host submits a regular message, the IMP checks for an existing simplex virtual circuit connection from the source host to the destination host, and opens one if there is none. There may be at most eight messages outstanding on that connection at any one time. If a host submits a ninth message before it receives a reply for the first, the host is blocked until that reply is sent. Connections stay open for some time but are timed out after three minutes of no activity, or can be closed if there is contention for the connection blocks at either end. A connection is never closed while messages are outstanding on it, which lets a source host count the replies it has received so that it can avoid being blocked by submitting a ninth outstanding message.

With an 1822L leader the same process occurs, except that connections are distinguished by the source port, source name and destination name combination. When the message arrives, the IMP first looks for an open connection for that same combination; if it finds one it uses it and performs no further name translation, and if it does not, it translates the destination name and opens a connection to the physical host port.
sections.plainLanguage: When a host starts up it and its IMP exchange a few no-op messages to get in step. After that, each pair of hosts has a connection that can carry eight messages at a time before the sender has to wait for a reply.

sections.title: The Host-to-IMP Leader Format
sections.content:
The 1822L host-to-IMP leader is 96 bits long. Bits 1 to 4 are unused and must be zero. Bits 5 to 8 hold the 1822L Host-to-IMP flag, which is set to decimal 13. Bits 9 to 16 hold the handling type, which is bit-coded to indicate the transmission characteristics of the connection the host wants; bit 9 is the priority bit, and messages with it on are treated as priority messages, while bits 10 to 16 must be zero. Bits 17 to 20 are unused and must be zero. Bit 21 is the trace bit, which designates the message for tracing as it moves through the network. Bits 22 to 24 are leader flags, of which bit 22 is available for the destination host and bits 23 and 24 are reserved and must be zero.

Bits 25 to 32 hold the message type. Type 0 is the regular message, which carries all host-to-host communication and has sub-types in bits 77 to 80: sub-type 0 is standard, where the IMP uses its full message and error control facilities and host blocking may occur, and sub-type 3 is the uncontrolled packet, where the IMP performs no message control functions and network flow and congestion control may cause loss. Type 1 is an error without a message ID, type 2 is host going down, type 3 is the Name Declaration Message, type 4 is the NOP, type 8 is an error with a message ID, type 11 is a Name Server Request and type 12 is a Port List Request. Types 5 to 7, 9 to 10 and 13 to 255 are unassigned.

The rest of the leader carries the source host in bits 33 to 48, the destination host in bits 49 to 64, the message ID in bits 65 to 76, the sub-type in bits 77 to 80 and 16 unused bits in bits 81 to 96. An NDM message carries its own format in the data portion: the first 16 bits give the number of 1822L names, followed by 32-bit entries in which the first 16 bits are the name and the second 16 bits are zero to mean the name should not be effective or one to mean it should be. An NDM with zero entries makes all of the host's current effective names non-effective.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message a host sends starts with a 96-bit leader. It says what kind of message this is, which host sent it, which host it is for, and gives the message a number so that a reply can be matched to it.

fields.name: Unused
fields.desc: Bits 1 to 4; must be set to zero.

fields.name: Handling Type
fields.desc: Bits 9 to 16; bit 9 is the priority bit, bits 10 to 16 must be zero.

fields.name: Trace Bit
fields.desc: Bit 21; designates the message for tracing through the network.

fields.name: Leader Flags
fields.desc: Bits 22 to 24; bit 22 is available for the destination host.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: Bits 25 to 32; type 0 regular, type 3 NDM, type 4 NOP, and so on.

fields.name: Source Host
fields.desc: Bits 33 to 48; the 1822L name or address of the sender.

fields.name: Destination Host
fields.desc: Bits 49 to 64; the 1822L name or address of the receiver.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Bits 65 to 76; matches a reply to this message.

fields.name: Sub-type
fields.desc: Bits 77 to 80; for a regular message, 0 is standard and 3 is uncontrolled packet.

cells: A physical host port: an 8-bit host number and a 16-bit IMP number. Used in 1822 leaders only.
A logical identifier for one or more hosts, independent of where they are. Bits 1 and 2 are not both zero.
A physical host port or an IMP fake host. A subset of the name space with bits 1 and 2 both off.

items.label: Regular Message
items.desc: All host-to-host communication. Sub-type 0 is standard and sub-type 3 is an uncontrolled packet.

items.label: Error Without Message ID
items.desc: An error report that does not name a message.

items.label: Name Declaration Message
items.desc: The host declares which of its 1822L names should be effective.

items.label: NOP
items.desc: Tells the IMP which style of leader the host wants to use.

items.label: Error with Message ID
items.desc: An error report that names the message it refers to.

items.label: Name Server Request
items.desc: Asks the IMP to translate a name and return the physical addresses it maps to.

items.label: Port List Request
items.desc: Asks the IMP which names it may use on this host port.
